passages.happening:
‘Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, who rely on horses, who trust in their abundance of chariots and in their multitude of horsemen’ (verse 1). ‘They do not look to the Holy One of Israel; they do not seek the LORD’ (verse 1).

Yet he too is wise. He brings disaster and does not take back his words. He will rise against the wicked and against those who help evildoers (verse 2).

‘But the Egyptians are men, not God; their horses are flesh, not spirit’ (verse 3). When the LORD stretches out his hand, the helper will stumble and the one he helps will fall; both will perish together.
passages.hearers:
This fourth woe of chapters 28 to 33 restates chapter 30 in a short form. Judah's leaders are still turning to Egypt for military help against Assyria. What is new is the clarity of the contrast. Verse 3 reduces the whole debate to one line: human beings against God, flesh against spirit.

The chapter belongs to the years around 705 to 701 BC, when Hezekiah's government was seeking an alliance with Egypt, then ruled by kings from Kush. Egypt was famous for its horses and chariots, the ancient world's most expensive and impressive military technology; Solomon had imported horses from there. To a small hill kingdom like Judah, an Egyptian chariot force would have looked like real security.

Verse 2 has a touch of irony. The leaders thought they were being wise. God too is wise, and his word does not fail.
passages.later: Jeremiah says the same: ‘Cursed is the man who trusts in mankind, who makes the flesh his strength and turns his heart from the LORD’ (Jeremiah 17:5). And Zechariah hears, ‘Not by might nor by power, but by My Spirit, says the LORD of Hosts’ (Zechariah 4:6).
passages.asks: Isaiah sets flesh against spirit, Egypt's horses against the Holy One. Ask what impressive help you rely on that is only flesh. And ask what it would mean to seek the LORD first rather than last.

passages.t: Like a lion, like hovering birds
passages.happening:
The LORD says that like a lion growling over its prey, not frightened off by a band of shepherds shouting at it, ‘so the LORD of Hosts will come down to do battle on Mount Zion and its heights’ (verse 4). ‘Like birds hovering overhead, so the LORD of Hosts will protect Jerusalem. He will shield it and deliver it; He will pass over it and preserve it’ (verse 5).

‘Return to the One against whom you have so blatantly rebelled, O children of Israel’ (verse 6). On that day every one of them will reject the idols of silver and gold their own hands made (verse 7).

‘Then Assyria will fall, but not by the sword of man; a sword will devour them, but not one made by mortals’ (verse 8). Their stronghold will pass away in terror and their princes panic at the battle standard, ‘declares the LORD, whose fire is in Zion, whose furnace is in Jerusalem’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Two pictures of God's protection sit side by side. The lion will not be scared off its prey by shouting shepherds; the LORD will not be scared off Zion by any army. And birds hovering over their nest protect their young. The verb pass over in verse 5 is the verb of the Passover, when God passed over Israel's houses in Egypt.

Verse 8 predicts that Assyria will fall not by a human sword. The book later records that the angel of the LORD struck the Assyrian camp in one night, and Sennacherib withdrew to Nineveh. Assyria's own records, as would be expected, do not mention a disaster; Sennacherib's annals claim a successful campaign and a large tribute from Hezekiah, but they do not claim the capture of Jerusalem. Assyria as an empire lasted nearly another century, until Nineveh fell in 612 BC.

The first hearers were called to return to the God they had rebelled against, and to throw away their idols. The promise of protection came with a call to repent.
passages.later: Moses sang of God, ‘As an eagle stirs up its nest and hovers over its young, He spread His wings to catch them’ (Deuteronomy 32:11). Isaiah records the night ‘the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 men in the camp of the Assyrians’ (Isaiah 37:36).
passages.asks: God is pictured as a lion that will not be scared off and as a bird hovering over its nest. Ask which of those pictures you need to believe today. And ask what idols you would throw away if you trusted that God would guard you.
